newsitem.title: UK: UK's Guardian newspaper launches on-line magazine.
newsitem.headline: UK's Guardian newspaper launches on-line magazine.

text.p: Britain's Guardian newspaper on Friday launched Shift Control, an online arts and lifestyle magazine designed exclusively for the Internet and aimed at 18- to 30-year-olds.

Guardian Newspapers, publisher of the Guardian and the Observer newspapers, opted to create a publication exclusively for the Internet, instead of making the entire contents of its newspapers available to on-line users.

"The idea was conceived out of a lot of discussions that took place in the Guardian and the Observer and how best to move forward in the on-line world," Robin Hunt, head of the Guardian's New Media Lab, told Reuters.
"I can imagine a world in which the daily newspaper works in tandem with the on-line world," he said.
Shift Control went live on Friday morning, but some users had problems accessing the full publication. An editor for Shift Control said there had been some glitches.

Hunt and Craig Wilkie, New Media publishing manager, jointly conceived the idea for Shift Control and then decided to seek a sponsorship partner. They approached Whitbread, the brewer and leisure group, and pitched their idea for an on-line magazine aimed at a hip, young audience -- the sort of people who read Arena and drink beer and are considered by advertisers as notoriously difficult to reach.

Both the Guardian and Whitbread are investing in Shift Control, but Hunt declined to detail the amount of the investment or the proportion contributed by each party. However, he called the Guardian's investment significant and said the company is committed to publishing Shift Control for one year.

The Guardian maintains total editorial control, with advertisements for Whitbread products included in various sections of the magazine. Each of the nine sections of the magazine will feature one Whitbread product. For instance, Rolling Rock beer will support Shift Control's weekly music round up, called Plug 'n Play.

Shift Control -- whose name is not only a pun on a computer command but also plays on the magazine's aim to interact with its readers by soliciting feedback and magazine contributions -- is being published on Fridays. It includes features, reviews, essays and fiction and a daily satirical, animated cartoon.

Hunt insisted that one of the things that will set Shift Control apart from its many on-line competitors is the quality of its writing. And while all the magazine's reviews are expected to be written by readers, Hunt said reviews will be carefully selected and edited and contributors will be paid.
Hunt said he had no idea how many readers Shift Control will attract. "I would hope lots," he said. "What I'm more keen on is the quality of people who come in."
A World Wide Web page developed by the Guardian earlier this year in tandem with the Euro '96 football championship attracted 500,000 users a day, he said.

There are no plans to charge readers for access to Shift Control. Hunt said there are other ways other than subscription revenue to build a financially successful publication, but he declined to elaborate.
The service can be accessed at the following address: WWW.SHIFTCONTROL.COM
